title: Examine Yourselves: Final Warnings and the Threefold Blessing
summary: Paul announces his third visit and warns that he will not spare those who continue in sin, since they demand proof that Christ speaks through him. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God's power, and Paul, weak in him, will live with him by that power. He urges the Corinthians to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith, prays for their restoration, and closes with a call to harmony and peace and a blessing in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit.
story: This is the last chapter of 2 Corinthians and the end of the section begun at chapter 10, where Paul has confronted the rival teachers and those in Corinth drawn to them. Chapter 12 ended with Paul's fear of finding quarreling and unrepented immorality when he arrives. Chapter 13 follows through with a final warning, but it ends not in severity but in blessing. What happened next is known only in outline: Paul did come to Corinth and stayed about three months (Acts 20:2-3), and it was there that he wrote his letter to the Romans, a sign that the relationship had held.
historical:
Paul had visited Corinth twice before: when he founded the church, around AD 50-51 (Acts 18:1-18), and on the painful visit mentioned in 2:1. This would be his third. His "second time" warning (verse 2) refers to that painful visit, when he had already warned those living in sin. Now, absent, he warns them again in writing so that when he comes he will not need to be severe.

About a generation later, around the end of the first century, the church in Rome wrote a letter to the church in Corinth (known as 1 Clement) because the Corinthians had deposed their leaders in another dispute. It shows that the church survived and remained a significant congregation, and that factional struggles continued to trouble it. Different Bible versions number the final verses differently: some combine verses 12 and 13, so that the closing blessing is verse 13 rather than verse 14.
cultural:
Verse 1 quotes Deuteronomy 19:15, the principle of Israel's law that no one could be convicted on the word of a single witness; every matter had to be established by two or three. Jesus applied the same principle to discipline in the community of his followers (Matthew 18:16). Paul may be using it to say that his warnings on successive visits count as witnesses, or that he will conduct any judgment with fair and proper evidence.

The "holy kiss" of verse 12 was a customary greeting among family members and close friends in the ancient Mediterranean world, and Paul asks Christians to greet one another this way as members of one family (also Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26). Calling it holy set it apart from mere social custom. It later became part of the liturgy in many early churches, where it was known as the kiss of peace.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-10 are the final warning, built around a cluster of words related to testing and proof (dokime, dokimazo, adokimos): the Corinthians demand proof of Christ in Paul (verse 3), but Paul turns the test back on them: "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves" (verse 5). He hopes they will see that he has not failed the test, but he would rather appear to fail than have them do wrong (verse 7). Verse 4 states the theology behind everything: weakness and power, crucifixion and life, in Christ and in his servants. Verses 11-14 are the letter closing, with a string of short commands, greetings, and finally the blessing of verse 14, which names the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit together.

outline.t: The third visit and the warning to those who sinned
Examine yourselves: authority for building up
The grace, love, and fellowship of the triune God

doctrines.note: Verse 14 is one of the clearest Trinitarian passages in the New Testament: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you." Paul does not define the Trinity, but he names Father, Son, and Spirit together as the source of every blessing, and the church's later confession grew from texts like this. It remains one of the most used benedictions in Christian worship.

"Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith" (verse 5). Faith is not merely a past decision but a present reality that can be examined. The test is whether "Jesus Christ is in you", a living relationship rather than a list of achievements.

Christ "was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God's power" (verse 4). The cross and resurrection are the pattern of the whole letter: God's power is shown through weakness, and death gives way to life.

words.note: Dokimazo, to test, examine, or prove, often used of testing metals to see if they are genuine. With its related words dokime (proof) and adokimos (failing the test), it runs through verses 3-7. The Corinthians had put Paul to the test; he asks them to test themselves.

Adokimos, failing the test, unapproved, counterfeit. It was used of coins or metals that failed assay. Paul uses it three times here. The question is not whether the Corinthians are perfect, but whether their faith is genuine.

Katartisis, restoration or perfection, found only here in the New Testament. Its related verb, used in verse 11 and translated "Aim for perfect harmony", can describe mending nets (Mark 1:19) or setting a bone. Paul's prayer is for the church to be restored, made whole.

Koinonia, fellowship, sharing, participation. In verse 14 "the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" can mean fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers, or participation in the Spirit himself; both are true to Paul's thought. The same word described the collection in 8:4.

christ: Verse 4 gathers up the message of the whole letter: Christ "was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God's power". The crucified and risen Jesus is the pattern for his servants, who are weak in him but will live with him by God's power. Christ is also present and at work: "Jesus Christ is in you" (verse 5), and he speaks through his apostle (verse 3). And in the closing blessing, "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ" stands first, before the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit, because it is through Christ's grace that believers come to know the Father's love and share in the Spirit.

hard.q: Does "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith" mean believers should constantly doubt their salvation?
hard.a:
The command has sometimes produced anxious introspection, with believers searching their hearts for proof they are truly saved and never finding enough. But Paul's point in context is different. The Corinthians were demanding that Paul prove his credentials; he turns the question around and asks them to consider their own standing. He expects them to pass: "Can't you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you?" The test he has in mind is whether Christ is present among them, not whether their lives are flawless.

Christian traditions have taught about assurance in different ways. Some emphasize that assurance rests chiefly on God's promises in Christ, with self-examination serving only to confirm it; others emphasize the evidence of a transformed life, or the inner witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16). Most would agree that healthy self-examination looks first to Christ, not to one's own performance, and that it is meant to lead to repentance and confidence, not to despair.

questions: Paul turns the Corinthians' demand for proof back on them. When are we quick to test others and slow to examine ourselves?
Paul would rather appear to fail than have the Corinthians do wrong. What does that reveal about the kind of leadership and love he has shown throughout this letter?
The closing blessing names the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Spirit. Which of the three do you most need to receive right now, and why?
